aspects.says: RecursiveAction suits in-place transformations and RecursiveTask suits results combined at join points.
aspects.reason: practised by the percent practice of the overview page 6.6.1, which uses a RecursiveTask for the maximum and a RecursiveAction to rescale in place

aspects.says: Each leaf of a counting RecursiveAction adds its local count to the one shared AtomicInteger, never replacing what other leaves added.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A RecursiveAction that counts adds each leaf's count to a shared AtomicInteger rather than to a plain int field.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: a lost update between a separate get and set cannot be forced by a test, so atomicity is not graded; count-matching grades that leaves add to the counter rather than overwrite it, and the quiz asks why the page counts locally and updates once

aspects.says: For very large arrays with many matches an AtomicLong avoids overflowing an AtomicInteger.
aspects.reason: a minor sizing note; a test would need an array of more than two billion matches

aspects.says: Arrays.parallelSetAll, parallelSort and parallelPrefix already run array work on the Fork/Join framework.
aspects.reason: a test sees only the resulting array, so it cannot tell whether an answer used a built-in or its own action; the page names them as alternatives to prefer, not as code to write

aspects.says: Subtasks that write an array work on strictly disjoint ranges [start, mid) and [mid, end), so they need no synchronization.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: invokeAll takes any number of subtasks or a collection and blocks until all of them complete, so their side effects can be read afterwards.
The two halves of a RecursiveAction's split run at the same time, as invokeAll(left, right) makes them.
Counting locally in the base case and updating the atomic once per leaf keeps contention low.
An action must not read data that other subtasks are modifying; reading a source and writing a separate destination avoids it.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A RecursiveAction is tested by checking its side effects, below, at and above the threshold.
aspects.reason: every practice on this page is graded exactly this way, by checking the array, counter or tree after the action; writing tests is not what a reader is asked to do

aspects.says: A RecursiveAction validates its input, such as a null array, in the constructor and fails fast.
A RecursiveAction's compute() returns void and produces its outcome by changing data in place.
invokeAll is preferred for a RecursiveAction because there is no result to compute inline, so fork-compute-join gains nothing.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
